title: Supervised Learning: Overview of Approaches
blurb: Tests the bias-variance trade-off and the inductive bias of each major algorithm family: linear models, SVMs, trees, KNN and Naive Bayes. Includes hand calculations and customer scenarios on choosing a first model.

ideas.title: Bias, variance and the train/test gap
Support vector machines: margin, C and kernels
No Free Lunch and fair model comparison

questions.prompt: In $\text{Expected Test Error} = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \text{Irreducible Error}$, which term can **no** choice of model or amount of data remove?
options: The sum of bias and variance, because they trade against each other
The variance term, because every sample differs a little
The irreducible error, because it is noise in the data itself
The bias term, because every model makes some assumption
questions.explanation: Irreducible error is noise in the data. No model removes it. Bias can be cut with a more flexible model, and variance with more data, regularisation or ensembling. The tempting answer, bias plus variance, is the part the trade-off works on. A good model choice shrinks that sum.

questions.prompt: Logistic regression computes $z = \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b$ and outputs $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$. Which statement is correct?
options: It outputs a hard class label only, so its decision threshold cannot be changed
It is a classifier that outputs $P(y=1 \mid x)$, and $z=0$ gives exactly 0.5
It is a regression model that predicts a continuous target such as price
It is a classifier whose output jumps sharply from 0 to 1 at exactly $z=0$
questions.explanation: Despite the name, logistic regression is a classifier. The sigmoid squashes any real $z$ into $(0,1)$, read as $P(y=1 \mid x)$, and $\sigma(0)=0.5$. The curve is smooth, not a step, so the output is a probability you can threshold anywhere (Listing 11.3).

questions.prompt: In a trained SVM, which training points determine where the decision boundary sits?
options: Only the misclassified points, which the model moves toward
The points farthest from the boundary, which anchor each class
Only the points closest to the boundary, the support vectors
Every training point, weighted equally
questions.explanation: The SVM picks the hyperplane with the widest margin to the nearest points of each class. Only those nearest points, the support vectors, fix the boundary. Every other point could move or vanish without changing it. That is the key difference from logistic regression, where every point contributes to the loss.

questions.prompt: What is the main weakness of a decision tree grown with no depth or leaf-size limit?
options: It is slow at prediction time because it scans every training row per query
It needs every feature standardised before it will split sensibly
It memorises training data, and small data changes give a different tree
It cannot model nonlinear relationships without manual feature engineering
questions.explanation: An unconstrained tree is the textbook high-variance model. It keeps splitting until it fits the training data, noise included, and a small change in the data gives a structurally different tree. Trees handle nonlinearity natively and do not need scaling. Scanning every training row at predict time is KNN's cost, not a tree's.

questions.prompt: Where does k-nearest neighbours pay for its flexibility?
options: At prediction time, where each query is compared with every training row
In bias, because it assumes the class boundary is a straight line
In interpretability, because its many coefficients are hard to read
At training time, because it fits many parameters by iteration
questions.explanation: KNN stores the training set and does its work when asked for a prediction. Each prediction computes a distance to every stored point, an $O(n)$ cost. That is why KNN's predict time (21.5 ms) was over twenty times any other model's in the Worked Example. It has no coefficients and makes no assumption about boundary shape, so it is low bias.

questions.prompt: What is the "naive" assumption in Naive Bayes?
options: Features are independent of each other given the class label
Every feature follows a normal distribution within each class
Features are independent of the class label, so priors dominate
Every class has the same prior probability before seeing data
questions.explanation: Naive Bayes assumes conditional independence: given the class, knowing one feature tells you nothing about another. That turns $P(x \mid y)$ into a product of per-feature likelihoods. Equal priors are not assumed. Normal likelihoods are a choice made by GaussianNB only. Features independent of the label would make the model useless.

questions.prompt: Which statement matches what the No Free Lunch theorem claims?
options: Averaged over all possible problems, no algorithm beats any other
On any single dataset, all well-tuned algorithms reach about the same accuracy
Simpler models always generalise better than more complex ones
Gradient-boosted trees beat every other family on any tabular dataset
questions.explanation: The theorem is an average over all possible problems. It rules out a universal favourite. It does not say algorithms tie on a given dataset. On real, structured data some families reliably win, for example Logistic Regression scored 1.000 on blobs and 0.289 on circles. "Boosted trees win on tabular data" is an empirical pattern, not the theorem.

questions.prompt:
A churn team reports two models.

| Model | Train accuracy | Test accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| A | 0.71 | 0.70 |
| B | 0.99 | 0.78 |

Which diagnosis and next step is correct for each, following Procedure 11.4?
options: Both underfit, because neither test score is above 0.80, so both need more flexibility.
A overfits, so simplify it. B underfits, so add features or a more flexible model.
B is better in every way, because its test score is higher, so no diagnosis is needed.
A underfits: use a more flexible model. B overfits: simplify, regularise or add data.
questions.explanation: Model A has both scores low and almost no gap. That is high bias. More flexibility or better features is the fix. Model B is high on train, much lower on test, a gap of 0.21. That is high variance. Simplify, regularise, get more data or ensemble. B does have the higher test score today, but the gap says it has room to improve by fixing variance.

questions.prompt: A logistic regression has weights $\mathbf{w} = (0.8, -1.5)$ and intercept $b = 0.4$. For a customer with $\mathbf{x} = (2, 1)$, what is $P(y=1 \mid x)$? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: $z = 0.8\times2 + (-1.5)\times1 + 0.4 = 1.6 - 1.5 + 0.4 = 0.5$. Then $\sigma(0.5) = 1/(1+e^{-0.5}) = 1/(1+0.6065) = 0.622$. A common slip is to report $z$ itself (0.5) as the probability.

questions.prompt: A linear SVM has $\mathbf{w} = (0.3, 0.4)$ and $b = -2$. The distance from a point to the hyperplane $\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b=0$ is $|\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b| / \lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert$. The training points are $(6,3)$ and $(8,4)$ in the positive class and $(2,1)$ and $(0,2)$ in the negative class. What is the margin, the distance from the boundary to the closest point of either class? Give a decimal to 1 d.p.
questions.explanation: $\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert = \sqrt{0.09+0.16} = 0.5$. Scores $\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b$: $(6,3)\to 1.0$, $(8,4)\to 2.0$, $(2,1)\to -1.0$, $(0,2)\to -1.2$. Distances: 2.0, 4.0, 2.0, 2.4. The closest points, $(6,3)$ and $(2,1)$, are both 2.0 away, so the margin is 2.0 and these two are the support vectors. Forgetting to divide by $\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert$ gives 1.0.

questions.prompt: Gini impurity of a node is $1 - \sum_k p_k^2$. A node holds 20 churners and 20 non-churners. A split sends 16 rows left (14 churners, 2 non-churners) and 24 rows right (6 churners, 18 non-churners). By how much does the split reduce Gini impurity, using the size-weighted average of the children? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: Parent: $1 - 0.5^2 - 0.5^2 = 0.5$. Left: $1 - (14/16)^2 - (2/16)^2 = 1 - 0.7656 - 0.0156 = 0.2188$. Right: $1 - 0.25^2 - 0.75^2 = 0.375$. Weighted: $0.4\times0.2188 + 0.6\times0.375 = 0.3125$. Reduction: $0.5 - 0.3125 = 0.1875 \approx 0.188$. Averaging the children without weights gives 0.297 and a reduction of 0.203, which is wrong.

questions.prompt:
A KNN regressor with $k=3$ and Euclidean distance uses these (already scaled) training points.

| Point | $x_1$ | $x_2$ | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 1 | 1 | 200 |
| B | 2 | 1 | 240 |
| C | 4 | 3 | 400 |
| D | 1 | 3 | 260 |
| E | 5 | 5 | 500 |

What does it predict for the query $(2, 2)$? Give a decimal to 1 d.p.
questions.explanation: Distances from $(2,2)$: A $\sqrt{2}=1.41$, B $1$, C $\sqrt{5}=2.24$, D $\sqrt{2}=1.41$, E $\sqrt{18}=4.24$. The three nearest are B, A and D. KNN regression averages their targets: $(240+200+260)/3 = 233.3$. Including C instead of D (a slip in the distance) gives 280.

questions.prompt: A tiny spam filter was trained on 10 emails: 4 spam, 6 not spam. The word "free" appears in 3 of the 4 spam and 1 of the 6 non-spam emails. The word "meeting" appears in 1 of the 4 spam and 4 of the 6 non-spam emails. A new email contains both words. Using only these two word-presence features and the Naive Bayes assumption, what is $P(\text{spam} \mid \text{free}, \text{meeting})$? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: Spam score: $P(\text{spam}) \times P(\text{free} \mid \text{spam}) \times P(\text{meeting} \mid \text{spam}) = 0.4 \times 0.75 \times 0.25 = 0.075$. Non-spam score: $0.6 \times \tfrac{1}{6} \times \tfrac{4}{6} = 0.0667$. Normalise: $0.075 / (0.075 + 0.0667) = 0.529$. Forgetting the priors gives $0.1875/(0.1875+0.1111) = 0.628$.

questions.prompt:
A colleague writes this before benchmarking.

```python
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X)
X_scaled = scaler.transform(X)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X_scaled, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=RANDOM_SEED
)
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_train, y_train)
print(clf.score(X_test, y_test))
```

What is wrong with it?
options: Logistic regression does not need scaling, so the scaler only adds bias to the fit.
Nothing. Scaling before splitting keeps train and test on one shared scale, which is required.
The scaler's mean and std were computed with the test rows, leaking test information into training.
`stratify=y` should be removed, because it leaks the label distribution into the split.
questions.explanation: Fitting the scaler on all of `X` lets the test rows shape the mean and standard deviation used to train. That is leakage, and it inflates the test score. The fix is Listing 11.1: put the scaler inside a `Pipeline` so it is fitted on training data only and applied, not refitted, to test data. Stratifying on `y` is standard and does not leak.

questions.prompt:
A customer tunes `max_depth` of a decision tree with 5-fold CV.

| max_depth | Train acc. | CV mean ± std |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 0.74 | 0.73 ± 0.01 |
| 5 | 0.86 | 0.84 ± 0.02 |
| 12 | 0.97 | 0.81 ± 0.04 |
| None | 1.00 | 0.78 ± 0.06 |

Their lead wants `None` because "it gets 100% on training data". What is the best reading?
options: Pick depth 5. Deeper trees gain train accuracy but lose CV accuracy, a variance sign.
Pick depth 2. Its tiny fold spread shows it will generalise best to new customers.
Pick `None`. Perfect training accuracy shows the tree has found the true boundary.
Pick depth 12. It is the best compromise between the train and CV accuracy.
questions.explanation: CV mean peaks at depth 5. Deeper trees raise train accuracy but lower CV accuracy, the gap widens (0.02, 0.16, 0.22) and the fold spread grows. Those are the high-variance symptoms from Procedure 11.4. Depth 2 is stable but both scores are low, which is high bias. Training accuracy never picks a model.

questions.prompt: A churn model is $P(\text{churn} \mid x) = \sigma(-2 + 0.5x)$, where $x$ is days since last login. Following Listing 11.3 the team flags a customer when the predicted probability is at least 0.3. What is the smallest $x$ that gets flagged? Give a decimal to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation: Invert the sigmoid. $\sigma(z) = 0.3$ when $z = \ln(0.3/0.7) = -0.847$. Solve $-2 + 0.5x = -0.847$, so $x = 1.153/0.5 = 2.31$. With the default 0.5 threshold the cut-off would be $z=0$, $x=4$. Lowering the threshold flags more customers, raising recall and lowering precision.

questions.prompt: An RBF-kernel `SVC(C=1000)` inside a scaling Pipeline gets training accuracy 1.00 and 5-fold CV accuracy 0.82 ± 0.06 on 3,000 rows. Which single change is most likely to help?
options: Raise `C` to 10,000 so fewer points violate the margin
Remove the `StandardScaler`, because the RBF kernel rescales internally
Switch to `LinearSVC` and keep `C=1000`, because linear models never overfit
Lower `C` so the margin widens and tolerates more violations
questions.explanation: Perfect training accuracy, a lower CV score and a wide fold spread point to high variance. A large $C$ gives a narrow margin that tolerates few violations (low bias, high variance). Lowering $C$ widens the margin and moves toward higher bias, lower variance. Raising $C$ makes the overfit worse. Removing scaling breaks the distance in the RBF kernel.

questions.prompt:
A node holds 20 positives and 20 negatives. The tree compares two candidate splits using size-weighted Gini impurity ($1 - \sum_k p_k^2$).

- Split A: left 10 rows (10 positive, 0 negative), right 30 rows (10 positive, 20 negative).
- Split B: left 20 rows (15 positive, 5 negative), right 20 rows (5 positive, 15 negative).

Which split does the tree choose?
options: Split B, with weighted Gini 0.375
Split B, because equal-sized children always give lower impurity
Neither, because both leave the weighted Gini at 0.5
Split A, with weighted Gini 0.333
questions.explanation: A: left is pure (Gini 0). Right: $1 - (1/3)^2 - (2/3)^2 = 0.444$. Weighted: $0.25\times0 + 0.75\times0.444 = 0.333$. B: each child $1 - 0.75^2 - 0.25^2 = 0.375$, weighted 0.375. Lower is better, so the tree picks A. Balanced children look tidier but do not guarantee lower impurity.

questions.prompt:
A 1-NN churn model uses raw features (age in years, annual income in dollars). Two training customers:

- P1: age 55, income 60,200, label *stays*
- P2: age 31, income 61,500, label *churns*

The query is age 30, income 60,000. Then the team applies min-max scaling using ranges age 20–70 and income 20,000–120,000. What does 1-NN predict before and after scaling?
options: Churns both times, because P2 is closer in age
Stays both times, because P1 is closer in income
Churns before scaling, stays after scaling
Stays before scaling, churns after scaling
questions.explanation: Raw: distance to P1 is $\sqrt{25^2+200^2} = 201.6$, to P2 is $\sqrt{1^2+1500^2} = 1500$. Income dominates, so P1 wins and the prediction is *stays*. Scaled: age differences divide by 50, income by 100,000. P1: $\sqrt{0.5^2 + 0.002^2} = 0.50$. P2: $\sqrt{0.02^2 + 0.015^2} = 0.025$. Now P2 is far closer and the prediction is *churns*. Without scaling, the feature with the largest units decides the neighbours.

questions.prompt: Take the same spam filter: priors 0.4 spam, 0.6 not spam. $P(\text{free} \mid \text{spam}) = 3/4$, $P(\text{free} \mid \text{not spam}) = 1/6$, $P(\text{meeting} \mid \text{spam}) = 1/4$, $P(\text{meeting} \mid \text{not spam}) = 4/6$. An engineer adds a third feature, "FREE in capitals", that in this data always appears exactly when "free" does, so it has the same likelihoods as "free". For an email with "free", "FREE" and "meeting", what posterior $P(\text{spam} \mid \cdot)$ does Naive Bayes now report? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: Naive Bayes treats the copy as new, independent evidence. Spam: $0.4 \times 0.75 \times 0.75 \times 0.25 = 0.05625$. Not spam: $0.6 \times \tfrac16 \times \tfrac16 \times \tfrac46 = 0.01111$. Posterior: $0.05625/(0.05625+0.01111) = 0.835$. The same email scored 0.529 before. Nothing new was learned, but the posterior jumped. This is the cost of conditional independence being false. Correlated features are double-counted, and posteriors become overconfident.

questions.prompt: A customer has 300 labelled rows. They run one stratified 80/20 split and report Random Forest 0.883 test accuracy and Logistic Regression 0.867. They plan to deploy Random Forest. What should you say first?
options: Switch to KNN, because it makes no assumption about the shape of the boundary.
Report the training accuracy instead, because 60 test rows are too few to judge.
Agree. A 1.6-point accuracy gain is meaningful on any dataset, so deploy it.
The gap is one test row of 60. Compare both with 5-fold CV in one Pipeline.
questions.explanation: The test set has 60 rows. 0.883 is 53/60 and 0.867 is 52/60, a difference of one row. A different split could reorder the ranking. Procedure 11.2 compares families with identical preprocessing and cross-validation, and reports mean ± std. If the scores overlap, the simpler, interpretable Logistic Regression is a sound default. Training accuracy never settles the choice.

questions.prompt: A screening model is $P(\text{malignant} \mid x) = \sigma(-4 + 0.02x)$, where $x$ is a lesion score. A missed malignancy costs 10 times as much as a false alarm. The clinic flags a case when the expected cost of not flagging exceeds the expected cost of flagging, $10p > 1\cdot(1-p)$. What is the smallest score $x$ that gets flagged? Give a decimal to 1 d.p.
questions.explanation: Flag when $10p > 1-p$, so $p > 1/11 = 0.0909$. The matching $z$ is $\ln\big(\tfrac{1/11}{10/11}\big) = \ln(0.1) = -2.3026$. Solve $-4 + 0.02x = -2.3026$, so $x = 1.6974/0.02 = 84.9$. The default 0.5 threshold would need $x = 200$. The cost ratio, not 0.5, sets the threshold, which is why a business-owned threshold matters (Listing 11.3).

questions.prompt: On the concentric-circles data from the Worked Example, standardised Logistic Regression scores 0.289. You must keep a linear model for audit reasons. Which change lets it separate the classes?
options: Raise `max_iter` to 10,000 so the solver can fully converge
Add the feature $r = x_1^2 + x_2^2$ so a threshold on $r$ is linear
Lower `C` so the model regularises harder and ignores noise
Remove the `StandardScaler` so the circles are no longer centred on the origin
questions.explanation: The classes differ by distance from the centre. In the original $(x_1, x_2)$ space no straight line separates them, however long the solver runs. Adding $r = x_1^2+x_2^2$ maps each point into a space where one hyperplane, $r = c$, splits the classes. In the original space that hyperplane is a circle. This is manual feature engineering, the explicit version of what the RBF kernel does implicitly. More iterations or stronger regularisation cannot change the model's inductive bias.

questions.prompt: A decision tree on 5,000 customers includes `customer_number`, a unique integer per row. With no depth limit it scores 1.000 on training data and 0.61 on test. Select ALL statements that are true.
options: Because trees do not need feature scaling, an ID column is harmless to them
Dropping the ID column and limiting depth or leaf size both attack the variance problem
Perfect training accuracy here says nothing about whether the tree learned real signal
Collecting more customers will make the `customer_number` splits generalise
The tree can split on `customer_number` until every leaf holds one row, so each leaf is pure
questions.explanation: A unique ID lets the tree isolate every row, so leaves become pure and training accuracy hits 1.000. That is memorisation, the high-variance failure mode, and the 0.61 test score confirms it. Scaling is irrelevant here. Trees ignore scale, but they do not ignore meaningless features. New customers get new IDs, so ID splits can never transfer. Removing the ID and constraining depth or `min_samples_leaf` are the right fixes.

questions.prompt: A retailer wants product recommendations from a KNN classifier trained on 2 million customers with 300 standardised features. Each request must return in under 10 ms. Select ALL statements that are true.
options: Adding more customers to the training set will lower prediction latency
With 300 dimensions, distances between points tend to become similar, so "nearest" carries less meaning
A tree ensemble or linear model is a sound alternative because its predict cost does not grow with the number of training rows
Each prediction computes a distance to all 2 million stored customers unless an approximate index is used
Training is the bottleneck for KNN, so a larger training instance solves the latency problem
questions.explanation: Plain KNN has an $O(n)$ cost per prediction, so 2 million rows is a latency problem. SageMaker's k-NN uses an approximate index for exactly this reason. With 300 features the curse of dimensionality weakens the notion of \"nearest\". More rows make each prediction slower, not faster. KNN does almost no work at training time, so a bigger training instance misses the bottleneck. Trees and linear models have predict costs set by their size, not by the training set.

bookExercises.prompt: For each of the following, name the algorithm family (Linear, Support Vector Machine, Tree-Based, Distance-Based, Probabilistic) and state its core assumption in one sentence: (a) spam detection using word-count features; (b) predicting house price from square footage and location; (c) classifying flowers from petal measurements using their five closest labelled neighbours.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: (a) Spam detection using word-count features: Probabilistic (Naive Bayes). Its core assumption is that features are conditionally independent given the class, which is a reasonable approximation for bag-of-words counts given a topic. (b) Predicting house price from square footage and location: Linear. Its core assumption is that the target is well-approximated by a linear combination of the input features. (c) Classifying flowers from petal measurements using their five closest labelled neighbours: Distance-Based (KNN). Its core assumption is that nearby points in feature space share a label, so a new point's class is decided by a majority vote among its closest training examples.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain, in your own words, why increasing model flexibility (e.g., letting a decision tree grow deeper) tends to reduce bias while increasing variance. Use the bias-variance equation from this chapter.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The equation is $\text{Expected Test Error} = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \text{Irreducible Error}$. A shallow tree can only express a small number of coarse if/else rules, so it's forced to represent the true decision boundary poorly no matter what training data it sees. That's high, stable bias. Letting the tree grow deeper adds more splits, so it can carve out increasingly fine-grained regions that match the true boundary more closely, which is exactly what lowers the bias term. But those extra splits are fit to the specific noise in the training sample, and a different training set would produce different deep splits, so the fitted function becomes unstable across resamples, which is exactly what raises the variance term. Flexibility is a dial on how much the model is allowed to bend to fit what it's shown, and bending further to reduce systematic error is the same mechanism that makes the fit more sensitive to which particular examples it saw.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the benchmark table in the Worked Example, identify the one algorithm whose test accuracy exceeds its CV mean accuracy, and explain what that ordering does, or doesn't, tell you about overfitting for that model.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Three algorithms in the benchmark table technically show test accuracy exceeding CV mean accuracy: Logistic Regression (0.982 vs. 0.980), Random Forest (0.956 vs. 0.954), and Decision Tree (0.912 vs. 0.910), and in every one of those three cases the gap is exactly +0.002. That uniformity is the point of the exercise: a gap of 0.002 is negligible next to the CV standard deviations reported alongside it (±0.013 for Logistic Regression, ±0.023 for Random Forest, ±0.019 for Decision Tree). The test score sits comfortably inside one CV fold's worth of ordinary variation for all three. This ordering tells you almost nothing about overfitting one way or the other; it just means this particular 80/20 test split happened to land on the easy side of average for those three models. A test score meaningfully below the CV mean, or a train/test gap computed directly (Procedure 11.4), is the diagnostic that actually signals overfitting. A tiny positive gap this size is noise, not evidence of a well-generalising model.

bookExercises.prompt: The Worked Example shows Decision Tree accuracy falling from 0.912 (30 features) to 0.789 (2 features), the largest drop of any algorithm. Using this chapter's description of how trees split, explain why restricting to two features hurts a tree more than it hurts Naive Bayes (0.930 → 0.877).
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A Decision Tree builds its predictions entirely out of axis-aligned splits on individual features, and its expressive power comes from chaining many such splits together: each additional feature gives it another axis to cut along, letting it carve out increasingly fine decision regions. Restricted to two features, the tree has nowhere left to turn: it can only ever partition a 2D plane with rectangular cuts, which is a drastic reduction in what shapes of boundary it can represent, and its accuracy collapses accordingly (0.912 → 0.789). Naive Bayes works completely differently: it multiplies together per-feature likelihoods under an independence assumption, so each feature contributes an essentially separate, additive piece of evidence to the final posterior. Dropping 28 of 30 features just means losing 28 pieces of independent evidence from a sum-like combination; the mechanism itself (multiply what evidence you have) still works exactly the same way with two features as with thirty, it just has less to work with. That's why Naive Bayes degrades gracefully (0.930 → 0.877) while the tree, which fundamentally needs many features to build its structure, degrades sharply.

bookExercises.prompt: A client has a 40,000-row tabular dataset with strongly nonlinear feature interactions and needs predictions to run inside a 5ms latency budget per request. Using Listing 11.1 and this chapter's Trade-offs table, name the algorithm you would rule out first, and explain why using the prediction-time numbers from the Worked Example.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Rule out K-Nearest Neighbours first. The Trade-offs table already flags KNN as "slow at predict time," and the Worked Example gives the concrete number: 21.5 ms to serve predictions on the held-out test set of only 114 samples drawn from a 455-row training set. That's over twenty times slower than every other algorithm's predict time, because KNN's prediction cost is $O(n)$ in the size of the training set (per Listing 11.1, every prediction requires a distance computation against every stored training point). Scaling from 455 to 40,000 training rows makes that cost far worse, not better: the per-request latency would grow roughly in proportion to the extra data, blowing well past the 5 ms budget even before accounting for the nonlinear-interaction requirement working against a distance metric already strained by many features. Random Forest or gradient-boosted trees, which handle nonlinear interactions natively and predict in single-digit milliseconds regardless of training set size, are the algorithms actually worth trying here.

bookExercises.prompt: The No Free Lunch theorem is often summarised as "no algorithm is better than any other." Using the blobs-vs-circles result (1.000 vs. 0.289 for Logistic Regression), explain why that popular summary is misleading for a working data scientist, and state the narrower claim the theorem actually makes.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "No algorithm is better than any other" implies a working data scientist should be indifferent between models, which is false and dangerous advice in practice: on the concentric-circles dataset, Logistic Regression scored 0.289, worse than a coin flip, while Random Forest scored a perfect 1.000, on the same data. Two algorithms performed wildly differently on one concrete problem; nothing about that result says "they're equally good on average across every problem," but it emphatically says they are not equally good on this problem, which is the one the data scientist actually has to solve. The narrower claim the theorem actually makes is that averaged over all possible problems, including ones with no structure whatsoever, unlike anything encountered in practice, no algorithm has an edge; it says nothing about the much smaller, highly structured set of problems real datasets belong to, where algorithms whose inductive bias matches the data's actual structure (a linear model on linearly-separable blobs, a tree ensemble on nonlinearly-separable circles) reliably win.

bookExercises.prompt: Read Burkov's Chapter 4 on the anatomy of a learning algorithm. Apply its three-part framework (hypothesis representation, loss function, optimisation procedure) to Naive Bayes, and explain what makes its optimisation step so much faster than logistic regression's.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only, no single answer. Applying Burkov's framework to Naive Bayes: the hypothesis representation is a set of per-feature conditional probability distributions, one likelihood distribution per feature per class (e.g. a Gaussian mean/variance for each numeric feature within each class for GaussianNB), combined multiplicatively via Bayes' theorem to produce a posterior over classes. The loss function is essentially absent in the sense logistic regression uses one: rather than defining an error to minimise and searching for parameters that reduce it, Naive Bayes' parameters are the maximum-likelihood estimates of each per-feature distribution, computed directly from counts or sample statistics. The optimisation procedure follows from that: since the independence assumption reduces parameter estimation to closed-form per-feature statistics (a mean and variance per class, or a frequency count per category), fitting is a single pass over the training data with no iteration. Contrast Logistic Regression, whose sigmoid-linked linear combination has no closed-form maximum-likelihood solution and requires an iterative convex optimiser (gradient descent or L-BFGS, controlled by `max_iter`) that repeatedly evaluates and adjusts every coefficient until convergence. That structural difference, closed-form counting versus iterative search, is exactly why Naive Bayes trains in roughly 2 ms while Logistic Regression takes roughly 5 ms on the same data, and the gap widens sharply as feature counts grow.
